title: When and Why Does Multi-Agent Debate Fail and Does It Really Underperform?
claim: Competitive and consensus-seeking protocols reach wrong verdicts through hacking, while a collaborative protocol reaches the right one at lower cost and with consistent gains.
layout: 2 panels: left dialogue columns with ✗/✓ verdicts, right scatter plot with broken y-axis
description: Panel (a) on the left starts with an error-detection problem. A user icon poses a math word problem task, a robot answers it, and a final 'No error' ground-truth verdict appears with a green check. Two dashed-separated columns follow. The first shows the original debater positions in blue and red speech bubbles, then Competitive MAD, where Alice's 'fundamentally flawed' rhetoric leads the judge to a wrong verdict, marked with a red X. The second shows Consensus-seeking MAD, where Bob echoes Alice and the judge is wrong, then Collaborative MAD, where Alice adds a new error and the judge is correct, marked with a green check. Robot icons label the roles. Panel (b) on the right is a scatter plot of change in F2 against log prompt tokens, with a broken y-axis. A large blue star for ColMAD sits above zero, while the other protocols sit below it.
caption: Comparison of different \mad protocols on error detection. (a) Given a task of checking whether an LLM-generated math problem meets all requirements, both \copmad and \cosmad exhibit debate hacking: \copmad debaters use overconfident rhetoric ("fundamentally flawed") to mislead the judge, while \cosmad debaters echo each other's opinion without challenge. \ours encourages debaters to complement missing evidence, enabling the judge to reach the correct verdict. (b) Change in average F2 over the stronger single agent against prompt tokens per sample on the six pairs of LLMs from Table [ref]. \ours is the only protocol whose mean is above the single agent and its worst pair is the mildest; \cosmad is cheap but below zero on average; \copmad loses 14 to 45 points on four of the six pairs and MP 24 and 40 on the two pairs with a reasoning model.
abstract: Multi-agent debate (MAD) was proposed as a promising approach for ensembling the wisdom of multiple large language models (LLMs) to improve reasoning and provide effective supervision to superhuman LLMs. However, increasing empirical evidence suggests that MAD may not outperform or even underperform single-agent approaches (SA), raising doubts about the benefits of MAD. In this work, we investigate this issue by analyzing the incentive structures of popular MAD paradigms: (i) competitive MAD (CopMAD) where agents compete by holding opposing positions; (ii) consensus-seeking MAD (CosMAD) where agents are driven to seek consensus. We show that both paradigms suffer from debate hacking: CopMAD reduces to a cheap-talk game, where agents produce misleading messages to win the game, while CosMAD filters out informative disagreements for premature consensus. Consequently, agents in both CopMAD and CosMAD fail to jointly resolve the ambiguity and seek the truth. To this end, we introduce ColMAD, a collaborative protocol that reframes MAD as a non-zero-sum game to encourage agents to provide informative while truthful messages. Through extensive benchmarking on challenging tasks such as error detection, we show that ColMAD consistently outperforms previous MAD protocols under multi-seed evaluation across heterogeneous LLM pairs. Under the same budgets, ColMAD effectively brings non-trivial improvements over SA methods, implying that the protocol design is critical to realizing the potential of MAD. The code is available at https://github.com/LFhase/ColMAD .
